root_question: What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?
input:
Inference-time steering of VLA internals (SAEs, FFN vectors, conceptors, linear observers)
Steering a VLA's internal features can bring out behaviour the model already has, without retraining. On real DROID hardware, SAE steering of pi0.5 raised target-object grasps by +9 to +21 out of 25 trials, and ablating the top-4 general features cut success from 39/40 to 0/40. COAST conceptors raised pi0.5 on LIBERO-10 from 0.43 to 0.80, with about +40% on three real tasks. Grant et al. found motor programs bound to absolute coordinates (50/50 grasps at the recorded spot on a UR10e). All tests are rigid tabletop tasks; none is cloth or a dish rack. Goodfire markets steering for robotics but publishes no numbers.
What more compute would buy: The quantity is closed-loop rollouts and SAEs swept; the largest is 420,000+ rollouts and 520+ SAEs across six VLAs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19233), and above that it is unknown whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour, because every sweep so far ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks.
What runs step after step: Each feature waits on an SAE fit (about 6,700 Adam steps, derived from https://arxiv.org/html/2603.19183; 'a few GPU-hours per SAE on one A100') and then on closed-loop rollouts of up to 300 steps, each waiting on a ~150 ms VLA forward pass and the next observation; the answer needed 150 rollouts × 135 features (20,250 episodes), and one unbatched rollout leaves the GPU idle while the simulator steps. Steps within a rollout must run in order, but rollouts are independent: batching hundreds of steered environments in a GPU-parallel simulator, with a separate hook per environment and simulation pipelined against inference, would run them together; this pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth). The nearest attempt is RLinf-VLA, 1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill environments, for RL rather than interpretability (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06710v2).
criterion: The question removes the closed-loop dependency: it scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes, and confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes.

root_question: Do more members of a machine-learned weather ensemble buy better forecasts of rare extremes, or does error shared by all members cap the skill?
input:
**ml-ensemble-extremes · Ensemble size for rare extremes in a machine-learned weather ensemble.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: the lever · PASS

**Question.** Does 10 to 1,000 AIFS-ENS members beat 50 for top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain probability forecasts, or does shared model error cap the skill?

**What is known.** HENS Part 2: 7,424 SFNO members per day for 92 summer-2023 dates; showed huge ensembles sample 4-sigma tails and reduce outliers. Whether AIFS-ENS, whose members are exchangeable draws of one afCRPS-trained distribution, keeps gaining skill past 50 members or saturates from shared model error.

**Hypothesis.** More members keep helping: 1,000 members sample top-percentile tails far better than 50, so extreme-event scores keep improving [s_hens].

**If compute is the lever.** Skill on top-percentile wind, temperature, and rain keeps rising past 50 members: 1,000 members sharpen the tails and improve extreme-event scores.

**If not.** Skill flattens near 50 members: members are exchangeable draws of one trained distribution, so shared model error caps tail sharpness and extra members add nothing.

**Test.** Run 7,000 fifteen-day AIFS-ENS v1 forecasts (7 dates x 1,000 members) on eight A100 40 GB GPUs; subsample 10-1,000 members, score top-percentile wind/temperature/rain probabilities against ERA5 with fair CRPS and Brier scores, and test whether skill still rises past 50 members.

*Compute axis.* Ensemble members per forecast: 10–1,000 members, 6 levels. Closest prior: 7,424 [s_hens], not beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Reproduce the published 4-minute N320 member time and 38 GB memory; one control run must match ECMWF open data within ensemble spread [s_crps_paper]. Tolerance: timing within +/-25% of 4 min; 38 GB memory fits; control field within the ensemble's own member-to-member spread at each lead time (GPUs are non-deterministic, so exact reproduction is not expected).

**Would not show.** Applies to AIFS-ENS v1 medium-range extremes on 7 dates; not a multi-season reforecast, other models, subseasonal leads, or direct proof that shared error causes any saturation.

*Cost.* Plans $963.17 of the $1,000 budget over 74.3 machine-hours, leaving $36.83. Main guess: peak filesystem usage [g], measured after $19.90 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 15× higher. Full scale: A 30-date multi-season reforecast at 1,000 members, $3,980, 3.98× the budget.

root_question: generative pipeline for discovery of single phase immersion coolants
input:
**IC-V1 · Force-field error floor for coolant MD: an enlarged C10–C50 benchmark scored against measurement.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · PASS

**Question.** Will graphics-card molecular simulations using Green–Kubo on C10–C50 hydrocarbons and esters rank immersion coolants' viscosity and thermal conductivity the same way measurements do?

**What is known.** Ogbomo and colleagues, in 2026, used Green–Kubo molecular dynamics to compute viscosity and thermal conductivity for eight C10–C50 molecules at 40 °C and compared with measurements [s_ogbomo_md]. Whether the error is a correctable bias or a random floor that caps ranking, and how rank agreement holds over hundreds of molecules [s_ogbomo_db].

**Hypothesis.** Green–Kubo MD with one fixed force field has a chemistry-dependent error floor near 25 percent that more molecules cannot remove [s_ogbomo_res].

**If compute is the lever.** At 120 molecules, held-out viscosity error after bias correction falls below 15 percent and rank correlation with measurement exceeds 0.9 [s_ogbomo_res].

**If not.** Held-out viscosity error stays above 25 percent and rank correlation below 0.7 at every set size, capping candidate ranking [s_ogbomo_res].

**Test.** One LAMMPS LOPLS-AA Green–Kubo protocol at 40 °C, six five-nanosecond replicas per molecule, run on 8, 24, 48 then 120 molecules from the public 835-molecule reference set, scored only against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity [s_ogbomo_db].

*Compute axis.* Benchmark molecules scored against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity: 8–120 molecules, 4 levels. Closest prior: 8 [s_ogbomo_md], beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Repeat the published eight-molecule Green–Kubo run first: density within 4% for seven molecules and thermal conductivity over-predicted for all eight [s_ogbomo_res]. Tolerance: same bias signs for viscosity and thermal conductivity; density error within 4 percentage points of the published error; per-molecule viscosity within 20% of the reference value.

**Would not show.** Shows transport-property error only at 40 °C for pure liquids between 1 and 50 mPa·s, not blends or sold coolants. Cannot show ranking behaviour beyond 120 molecules.

*Cost.* Plans $940.98 of the $1,000 budget over 59 machine-hours, leaving $59.02. Main guess: assumed MD throughput per GPU [p], measured after $36.20 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 1.1× lower. 3 cost flags in the block.
